analysis.one_liner: Holds private equity funds liable for company debts and taxes fund managers' carried interest as ordinary income.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee: referred there in July 2019, it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrote the rules for private equity, the investment funds that buy controlling stakes in companies. It would make funds financially responsible for the debts, legal penalties, and pension obligations of the companies they control, block a bought company from paying big dividends back to the fund for two years, and move workers' owed wages, severance, and pensions closer to the front of the line in bankruptcy. It would also close the carried interest loophole, which lets fund managers pay a lower tax rate on their share of fund profits, and require funds to disclose their fees and returns to investors.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at the roughly 5.8 million jobs the bill's findings say are at companies owned by private equity funds would gain the most: owed wages and severance would rank higher in bankruptcy, executive bonuses during bankruptcy would be restricted, and courts would have to weigh job preservation when approving asset sales. Pension funds and other investors would get standardized fee and return disclosures and stronger fiduciary duties. Taxpayers would gain from fund managers' profits being taxed at ordinary income rates instead of lower capital gains rates.

how_it_helps.text: Makes a private equity fund, and its investors, jointly and severally liable for the debts, legal penalties, WARN Act violations, pension withdrawal liabilities, and Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation claims of companies the fund controls.

Prohibits a company a private fund has acquired from paying dividends, buybacks, or similar capital distributions to the fund for two years after the takeover, and lets employees and creditors sue to claw back transfers made in violation.

Doubles the wage priority in bankruptcy from $10,000 to $20,000 per worker, adds severance pay and employee benefit contributions as priority claims, and treats unpaid wages and benefit contributions as costs recoverable from collateral.

Restricts executive bonuses, retention pay, and compensation enhancements during bankruptcy unless a court finds them essential and not disproportionate to what the nonmanagement workforce receives, and requires courts to weigh job preservation when approving asset sales.

Treats carried interest — the share of fund profits paid to fund managers — as ordinary income taxed at regular rates, instead of at lower capital gains rates, and imposes a surtax on payments from controlled companies to investment firms.
Requires private funds to publicly disclose fees and returns, imposes fiduciary obligations on them, and gives gift card holders a bankruptcy claim of up to $1,800.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity funds, their managers, and their wealthy investors would bear the cost: personal and fund-level liability for portfolio company obligations, a two-year ban on extracting dividends, a new surtax, higher taxes on carried interest, and disclosure requirements. Lenders that package risky corporate debt would have to retain a share of the risk they securitize.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity funds and their investors

drawbacks.text: The joint and several liability extends to every holder of an economic interest in a controlling fund, not just the fund's managers, which could make passive investors — including pension funds — reluctant to commit capital to buyout funds and raise the cost of capital for the companies involved.

The two-year dividend prohibition and tighter limits on deducting business interest at highly leveraged companies could deter private funds from buying struggling firms at all, leaving some companies without any rescue investment.

The carried interest changes reach any investment services partnership interest, including real estate and other investment partnerships beyond classic private equity, which broadens the tax increase beyond the fund managers the bill's title targets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, retirees, and taxpayers the benefits were concrete and large: wages and pensions that currently get pushed behind other creditors in bankruptcy would rank higher, and a lower tax rate reserved for a small group of fund managers would end. The design risks are real but secondary: sweeping liability and restrictions could reduce buyout investment in marginal companies, and critics of carried interest reform generally note the tax change reaches more of the investment industry than private equity alone. On balance the bill's costs fall on a concentrated industry while its benefits are broadly distributed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on July 17, 2019 with Senators Baldwin, Gillibrand, Brown, and Sanders as original cosponsors.
The bill's findings cite nearly 5.8 million people working for companies owned by private equity funds and a wave of retail bankruptcies including Sears, Toys "R" Us, and Payless ShoeSource.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced.
No further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity funds and their managers came out ahead: the carried interest tax treatment, the freedom to take dividends from acquired companies, and the existing limits on liability all remained in place. Workers and pension holders at private equity-owned companies gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity firms and fund managers

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Wall Street Looting Act and recruited four colleagues to cosponsor it on day one.

for.name: Sens. Tammy Baldwin, Kirsten Gillibrand, Sherrod Brown, and Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only Senate support it ever received.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — it received no hearing, no markup, and no committee vote for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: As the senator who controlled which bills reached the Senate floor, never brought the bill up for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sanders; no Senate Republican signed on, and the Republican-led Finance Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill targets the fund model directly: funds and their investors would be personally liable for portfolio companies' debts, penalties, and pension obligations, dividends extracted from acquired companies would be banned for two years, and a surtax would apply to payments from controlled companies. Workers at acquired firms currently absorb losses when buyouts fail while funds collect fees either way.

industries.industry: Hedge fund and investment fund managers
industries.note: Carried interest — fund managers' share of profits — would be taxed as ordinary income instead of at lower capital gains rates, eliminating a tax benefit available mainly to this group.

industries.industry: Banks and securitizers of leveraged corporate debt
industries.note: The bill requires firms that securitize risky corporate loans to retain a share of the risk they sell to investors, reducing a fee-driven business that currently passes losses to others.

industries.industry: Pension funds as private equity investors
industries.note: Many pension funds invest in private equity, so sweeping joint and several liability could reach them and raise the risk of committing capital; at the same time, the bill's disclosure and fiduciary provisions would give them better information and protections than they have now.
